screens.title: Troubleshooting Complex Routing Issues
screens.narratorSegment: Routing protocols are the nervous system of an enterprise network. In this lesson you will learn to diagnose why OSPF neighbors fail to reach full adjacency, why EIGRP neighbors refuse to exchange routes, and why BGP peers never reach the Established state. We focus on the practical causes you will see in the field: timer mismatches and MTU issues for OSPF, AS and K-value mismatches for EIGRP, and TCP, source-interface and authentication problems for BGP. You will also learn how redistribution can accidentally create routing loops or suboptimal paths if metrics, administrative distance, or route tags are not handled carefully. Throughout the chapter you will use targeted show and debug commands to collect evidence, then apply minimal, safe configuration changes to restore adjacency and correct path selection. Concrete examples include an OSPF adjacency stuck in INIT due to a hello timer mismatch and a mutual redistribution setup that requires a seed metric and the OSPF subnets keyword. By the end, you will be able to interpret adjacency state machines, spot mismatched parameters quickly, and protect redistribution with tags and proper metrics. Consider how a single mismatched timer or forgotten subnets keyword could cause a large outage — this is why disciplined verification and tagging matter.

screens.title: OSPF Adjacency States
screens.narratorSegment: OSPF neighbors walk through a defined sequence of states before they exchange link-state information. The states are Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading and Full. Each state signals a specific step in neighbor discovery or database synchronization. For example, Init indicates that a Hello packet was received but bidirectional communication hasn’t been established; 2-Way means bidirectional Hello reception has been confirmed, commonly on a multi-access network where DR/BDR elections matter. ExStart and Exchange are where master-slave roles and database description packets are negotiated. If a neighbor stalls in ExStart, a likely culprit is MTU mismatch: routers attempt to exchange DBD packets that the peer cannot process due to packet size differences. Full is the goal — it means complete adjacency and LSDB synchronization. A concrete example: you see a neighbor stuck in INIT on R1. That tells you R2’s Hellos reach R1, but R1’s Hellos are not acknowledged. Start with show ip ospf neighbor and show ip ospf interface to compare timers and interface parameters. A common misconception is to immediately reset interfaces; instead, collect evidence first. The key takeaway is that state transitions narrow the fault domain: read the state, correlate with expected packet exchange, and then target the parameter most likely to differ.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › OSPF Adjacency States
Definition

OSPF neighbor state machine

Each state indicates which packets have been sent and acknowledged. Use the state to decide the next verification command.

Init → 2-Way
Init shows Hellos received; 2-Way confirms bidirectional Hellos and DR/BDR election context.
ExStart / Exchange
Negotiation of master/slave and DB Description. MTU mismatches often appear here.
Loading → Full
Link-state databases are exchanged; Full means adjacency is complete.
Key Takeaway

Read the OSPF state first. It tells you whether to check Hellos, MTU, or LSDB exchange steps.

Evidence & Commands
show ip ospf neighbor
show ip ospf interface <interface_type/number>
debug ip ospf adjacency  (use with caution)
Concrete Example
Neighbor stuck in INIT. Use show ip ospf interface to compare hello/dead timers; correct mismatches and wait for Full state.
Common Mistake
Restarting routing processes without gathering state information can hide the root cause. Always collect evidence first.

screens.title: Common OSPF Configuration Mismatches
screens.narratorSegment: When an OSPF adjacency fails to form, there are a few repeat offenders: mismatched hello or dead timers, inconsistent network types, area ID differences, and authentication mismatches. Each has a distinct troubleshooting pattern. Start with show ip ospf neighbor to see the state. Then use show ip ospf interface to display hello and dead timers, network type, and whether authentication is active. If timers differ, either set the neighbor to the expected default or align both sides to match. Network types such as Broadcast, NBMA or Point-to-Point must agree on each end; a mismatch can prevent adjacency or change DR/BDR expectations. Area IDs must also match for interfaces participating in the same segment; an incorrect area ID isolates the neighbor relationship. Authentication is often overlooked: if one router is configured with authentication and the other is not, or if key chains differ, Hellos will be rejected. A practical approach is a short checklist: check neighbor state, compare timers, verify network type, confirm area ID and inspect authentication settings. A common misconception is assuming only MTU causes ExStart problems; in multi-access segments an incorrect network type can cause 2-Way behavior that prevents full adjacency. Always verify every listed parameter systematically.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Common OSPF Configuration Mismatches
Checklist

Step-by-step verification

  1. Run show ip ospf neighbor and note the state.
  2. Use show ip ospf interface <if> to read hello/dead timers and network type.
  3. Compare area IDs on both sides; ensure they match.
  4. Verify authentication configuration and keys match if enabled.
Misconception
Don't assume only MTU causes ExStart issues. Network type or timers may equally prevent progress.
Commands
show ip ospf neighbor
show ip ospf interface <interface_type/number>
show ip interface <interface_type/number>
debug ip ospf adjacency  (use carefully)
Example Fix
If R2 has ip ospf hello-interval 5 and R1 uses default 10, align timers by removing the custom hello interval or setting both to the same value.
Why it matters
Mismatches silently stop route exchange. A single forgotten authentication setting can keep an entire LSDB from synchronizing.

screens.title: OSPF MTU and ACL Issues
screens.narratorSegment: MTU mismatch is a subtle but frequent reason OSPF neighbors stall in ExStart. During ExStart/Exchange routers send database description packets which must fit within the peer's MTU. If the peer's MTU is smaller and cannot receive or process the DBD packets, the routers will never progress to Loading and Full. Use show ip interface to inspect interface MTU values and compare both ends. Adjust MTU only when you understand the downstream effects; often fixing tunnel or encapsulation settings that reduce MTU is safer than increasing interface MTU. Another frequent operator error is an access control list that blocks OSPF multicast addresses (224.0.0.5 for AllSPFRouters, 224.0.0.6 for AllDRouters) or blocks unicast packets needed for adjacency negotiation. Before changing ACLs, test connectivity with ping and confirm packet drops with counters. A common misconception is that only multicast must be allowed — OSPF also uses unicast for certain exchanges, and filtering can break adjacency. Always verify with show ip ospf neighbor and debug ip ospf adjacency while in a controlled window. The takeaway is to check MTU and ACLs as part of ExStart troubleshooting and to avoid blind interface resets without evidence.

keyIdea.text: ExStart stalls often indicate MTU issues; ACLs that filter OSPF multicast or unicast will also prevent adjacency formation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › OSPF MTU and ACL Issues
MTU Mismatch

Why ExStart stalls

DBD packets must fit the peer's MTU. If they don't, DBDs are dropped and adjacency cannot proceed.

show ip interface <interface_type/number>
  (compare MTU values on both ends)
Practical tip
If tunnels or encapsulation reduce effective MTU, address the encapsulation or adjust segmentation rather than arbitrarily raising MTU.
ACLs and OSPF

Blocking OSPF traffic

ACLs that block OSPF multicast (224.0.0.5 / 224.0.0.6) or relevant unicast ports will prevent neighbor formation or LSDB exchange.

Quick checks
  • Ping the neighbor IP to verify IP reachability.
  • Inspect interface ACLs and global ACLs for multicast or TCP/OSPF-related filtering.
  • Use counters and debug only in maintenance windows.

screens.title: EIGRP Neighbor Formation
screens.narratorSegment: EIGRP forms neighbors using Hello packets and requires matching Autonomous System numbers. If two routers are intended to be neighbors but do not appear in the neighbor table, the first checks are AS number, interface reachability and whether the interface is configured as passive. The command show ip eigrp neighbors reveals active neighbors; show ip protocols confirms the configured AS. If the AS numbers do not match, routers ignore each other even when IP reachability exists. Another important cause is a passive-interface configuration, which suppresses sending Hellos from that interface and therefore prevents neighbor formation. Authentication mismatches or ACLs blocking EIGRP multicast address 224.0.0.10 also break neighbor discovery. A concrete example: two routers with reachability but no neighbor entry. Run show ip protocols to verify AS, then show ip eigrp interfaces detail to check K-values and interface state. A common misconception is that K-values only affect metric calculation — in fact, mismatched K-values will prevent route exchange even if neighbor adjacency forms. The practical process is: verify AS, check passive-interface and ACLs, then confirm K-values and authentication before assuming a deeper software bug.

keyIdea.title: EIGRP fundamentals
keyIdea.text: Neighbors require the same AS number and active Hellos; passive interfaces, ACLs, or mismatched authentication block neighbor formation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › EIGRP Neighbor Formation
Definition

How neighbors appear

EIGRP uses Hellos; AS numbers must match. If there's no neighbor entry, verify AS, ACLs, and passive interfaces first.

show ip eigrp neighbors
show ip protocols
show ip eigrp interfaces detail
Example
Two routers on the same network but no neighbor entry. Check for passive-interface or mismatched AS on one side.
Pitfalls

K-values and authentication

K-values affect metric compatibility. If K-values differ, routers may form adjacency but will not exchange routes. Authentication mismatches silently block updates.

Commands to inspect
show ip eigrp interfaces detail (for K-values), show running-config for authentication and passive-interface settings.

screens.title: EIGRP K-values and Passive Interface Issues
screens.narratorSegment: EIGRP uses multiple coefficients, known as K-values, to calculate composite metrics. While neighbor formation primarily requires AS match and Hellos, exchanging routes requires compatible metric calculation parameters. If K-values configured on two routers differ, they will not accept route updates from each other. This is sometimes mistaken for a neighbor problem when actually the neighbors are present but routes are refused. To check K-values use show ip eigrp interfaces detail and compare the K-coefficients on participating interfaces. Passive-interface is another common operational setting that disables Hellos on an interface and thus prevents neighbor discovery. Operators sometimes mark an interface passive to stop route advertisements for security; however, if you expect neighbors on that interface, remove passive-interface or limit it to interfaces that should not form neighbors. Authentication mismatches also silently drop updates—always inspect key-chains and match types. A practical troubleshooting sequence: confirm neighbors in show ip eigrp neighbors, check K-values and authentication, and verify passive-interface settings. Closing question: when you see neighbors but no routes, do you check K-values first or authentication? Both are quick checks and together resolve the majority of EIGRP route-exchange issues.

keyIdea.text: Neighbors can exist without route exchange when K-values or authentication differ; passive-interface suppresses neighbor formation entirely.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › EIGRP K-values and Passive Interface Issues
K-values

Metric compatibility matters

If K-values differ, route updates are rejected even when neighbors exist. Confirm via show ip eigrp interfaces detail.

Example check
Compare K-coefficients on both peers; align them to allow routes to be accepted.
Passive Interface

Suppressing Hellos

A passive-interface prevents Hellos and neighbor formation. Verify running-config and show ip eigrp interfaces to find passive settings.

Common mistake
Operators sometimes set passive-interface for security but forget to allow necessary neighbors on adjacent segments.
Verification
show ip eigrp neighbors, show ip eigrp interfaces detail, and check key-chains for authentication mismatches.

screens.title: BGP Peering States and TCP Reachability
screens.narratorSegment: BGP neighbors move through states Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm and Established. These states reflect TCP connection progress and the BGP Open message exchange. When a BGP session never reaches Established, a basic test is to verify TCP reachability to port 179 using telnet or an equivalent test. If TCP cannot connect, an ACL or firewall is likely blocking BGP. If TCP connects but BGP stalls in OpenSent or OpenConfirm, inspect remote-as settings and authentication. The command show ip bgp summary provides a compact view of peer states and prefixes learned, while show ip bgp neighbors gives in-depth information including configured remote-as, authentication and update-source settings. A practical example: a neighbor stuck in Connect indicates TCP cannot complete; telnet <neighbor_ip> 179 fails. Confirm routing reachability with ping, then check ACLs and firewall rules. A common misconception is that BGP problems are always BGP-specific — often they are caused by basic IP reachability or TCP filtering. The diagnostic workflow is: ping the neighbor, test TCP port 179, inspect show ip bgp summary, and finally review neighbor configuration for remote-as and authentication mismatches.

keyIdea.title: Start with TCP
keyIdea.text: BGP often fails because TCP to port 179 is blocked or unreachable. Verify basic reachability before deeper BGP debugging.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › BGP Peering States and TCP Reachability
BGP States

From Idle to Established

States reflect TCP and BGP message exchange progress. Use show ip bgp summary to see peer state quickly.

show ip bgp summary
show ip bgp neighbors <neighbor_ip>
TCP Checks

Test connectivity to port 179

If telnet to port 179 fails, investigate ACLs, firewalls or routing that block or misroute BGP TCP sessions.

Concrete example
If a peer is stuck in Connect, ping first, then telnet <neighbor_ip> 179. If telnet fails, there is a TCP-level blockage to resolve before BGP can form.

screens.title: BGP Source Interface and ebgp-multihop
screens.narratorSegment: BGP sessions using loopback addresses require explicit source configuration because the TCP session source is not the physical interface IP. The update-source command sets the interface whose IP will be used as the TCP source address. If the neighbor expects a session from the loopback IP but you do not configure update-source, the remote router may reject the connection or fail the remote-as check. Additionally, eBGP peers that are not directly connected need ebgp-multihop to increase the TTL so TCP packets survive intermediate hops. When troubleshooting, verify that the neighbor is IP reachable from the configured source address; use ping with a source when possible and confirm routing to the source. If TCP connects but BGP fails authentication, inspect MD5 key-chains. A practical checklist: confirm reachability to the neighbor IP, verify the update-source is set when using loopbacks, use ebgp-multihop for non-direct eBGP peers, and confirm remote-as numbers match. A common mistake is to forget to route to the loopback source address from the peer, which makes TCP attempts originate from an unreachable IP. Always ensure symmetric reachability and matching TTL settings for eBGP multihop sessions before assuming a BGP implementation bug.

A practical checklist: confirm reachability to the neighbor IP, verify the update-source is set when using loopbacks, use ebgp-multihop for non-direct eBGP peers, and confirm remote-as numbers match. A common mistake is to forget to route to the loopback source address from the peer, which makes TCP attempts originate from an unreachable IP. Always ensure symmetric reachability and matching TTL settings for eBGP multihop sessions before assuming a BGP implementation bug.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › BGP Source Interface and ebgp-multihop
Update-source

Using loopbacks

Set update-source to use the loopback IP as the TCP source. Ensure the remote peer has a route back to that loopback address.

Verification
Ping the loopback from the neighbor and use traceroute to confirm symmetric reachability. Test TCP to port 179 from the source address if possible.
ebgp-multihop

When peers are not directly connected

Configure ebgp-multihop to increase TTL for eBGP peers across multiple hops. Check that intermediate ACLs allow TCP 179.

Common mistake
Forgetting to route to the loopback source or to allow TCP/179 through intermediate devices makes sessions fail even with update-source configured.

screens.title: BGP Route Filtering and Prefix Controls
screens.narratorSegment: Route-maps and prefix-lists are powerful tools to shape BGP advertisements, but incorrect filters can block all routes unintentionally. When peers are up but no routes are exchanged, inspect applied route-maps and prefix-lists for overly broad denies. The command show ip bgp summary shows prefixes learned; show ip bgp displays the BGP table. If the peer is Established but no routes appear, check outbound and inbound route-maps, neighbor prefix-list configuration and any distribute-lists. Another common issue is a route-map that depends on a tag or community that is not present; the result is an effective deny for every prefix. A safe troubleshooting sequence is: verify the peer is Established, temporarily remove or replace filters with a permissive rule to confirm behavior, and then reapply targeted filters. Remember that BGP filters can exist on both sides of the session; coordinate with the neighbor operator when possible. The takeaway is to treat filters as suspect when route counts drop unexpectedly and to use permissive testing before making permanent changes. BGP Route Filtering and Prefix Controls means when peers are established but no routes are present, inspect route-maps and prefix-lists for unintended denies and test with permissive rules.. In practical terms, how route-maps and prefix-lists can silently block advertisements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Inspection

Look for broad denies

Check inbound/outbound route-maps, prefix-lists and distribute-lists. A single deny can drop all prefixes if ordering is wrong.

show ip bgp summary
show ip bgp
show running-config | section neighbor
Safe testing

Use permissive rules first

Coordination tip

screens.title: Route Redistribution Principles
screens.narratorSegment: Redistribution allows different routing protocols to exchange routes, but it introduces risks: routing loops and suboptimal path selection. When you redistribute, remember that different protocols use different metrics and administrative distances. External routes introduced into another protocol often receive default metrics or higher administrative distance, which affects route selection. For example, OSPF may treat redistributed external routes differently unless you specify a seed metric. The seed metric is the initial metric you provide during redistribution so the target protocol can advertise a meaningful cost. Use route tags to prevent loops during mutual redistribution. Tag routes when they enter a protocol, and filter on that tag when redistributing back, so you don’t reintroduce the same route into its origin protocol. Also be mindful of OSPF: when redistributing into OSPF you usually need the subnets keyword to include subnetted routes. Troubleshooting techniques include show ip protocols to review redistribution configuration, show ip route to confirm path selection and debug ip routing cautiously to observe updates. The common mistakes to avoid are forgetting the subnets keyword, not setting an appropriate seed metric, and failing to apply tags — each can cause black holes, loops or unexpected path preferences.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Route Redistribution Principles
Definition & Risks

Why redistribution can be hazardous

Protocols use different metrics and administrative distances; careless redistribution can create loops or prefer suboptimal routes.

Administrative Distance
External routes often have higher AD; routers may prefer internal protocol routes over redistributed ones.
Seed Metric
Provide a metric when redistributing so the target protocol can advertise meaningful costs (examples vary by protocol).
Route Tags
Tag redistributed routes and filter by tag to prevent re-redistributing the same routes back into their origin protocol.
Practical rule

Test redistribution in a lab, always set explicit metrics and tags, and use the OSPF subnets keyword when redistributing subnetted routes into OSPF.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: OSPF INIT and Mutual Redistribution
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through the supplied lab scenario: R1 and R2 are connected on GigabitEthernet0/1. R1 runs OSPF Area 0 and R2 runs EIGRP AS 100, but the OSPF adjacency is stuck in INIT. The first diagnostic step is to run show ip ospf neighbor and show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/1 on both routers. These commands will reveal whether Hellos are mismatched. In the given initial configuration, R2 had ip ospf hello-interval 5 while R1 used the default of 10, so R1 saw R2’s Hellos but R2 did not accept R1's, resulting in INIT. Fix the mismatch by setting R2's hello interval to 10 or removing the custom hello command. Verify the adjacency reaches FULL with show ip ospf neighbor. Next, configure EIGRP AS 100 on R2 and advertise its networks. Then perform mutual redistribution on R2: redistribute ospf 1 metric 10000 100 255 1 1500 into EIGRP and redistribute eigrp 100 subnets metric 100 into OSPF. The redistribute commands must include a seed metric for EIGRP and the subnets keyword for OSPF. After configuration, verify route exchange using show ip route on both routers. A common pitfall is forgetting the subnets keyword or not providing a seed metric — both prevent expected route advertisement. Finish by checking that tags are applied if you plan mutual redistribution in production.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Lab Walkthrough
Problem

OSPF stuck in INIT

Start with show ip ospf neighbor and show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/1 on both R1 and R2 to identify parameter mismatches.

! R1 initial configuration
R1(config)# router ospf 1
R1(config-router)# network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
R1(config-router)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R1(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.1 255.255.255.0
R1(config-if)# no shutdown

! R2 initial configuration (problematic)
R2(config)# router ospf 1
R2(config-router)# network 10.0.12.0 0.0.0.255 area 0
R2(config-router)# interface GigabitEthernet0/1
R2(config-if)# ip address 10.0.12.2 255.255.255.0
R2(config-if)# ip ospf hello-interval 5
R2(config-if)# no shutdown
Fix & Redistribution

Commands to apply

Correct the hello interval on R2, then configure EIGRP and mutual redistribution with a seed metric and the subnets keyword.
! Fix OSPF hello mismatch on R2
R2(config-if)# no ip ospf hello-interval 5

! Configure EIGRP and redistribute on R2
R2(config)# router eigrp 100
R2(config-router)# network 10.0.20.0 0.0.0.255
R2(config-router)# redistribute ospf 1 metric 10000 100 255 1 1500
R2(config-router)# exit

R2(config)# router ospf 1
R2(config-router)# redistribute eigrp 100 subnets metric 100
R2(config-router)# exit
Verification
Use show ip ospf neighbor, show ip route on both R1 and R2 to confirm OSPF reaches FULL and routes are exchanged. Remember to use show ip protocols to review redistribution settings.

fullNarratorScript:
Routing protocols are the nervous system of an enterprise network. In this lesson you will learn to diagnose why OSPF neighbors fail to reach full adjacency, why EIGRP neighbors refuse to exchange routes, and why BGP peers never reach the Established state. We focus on the practical causes you will see in the field: timer mismatches and MTU issues for OSPF, AS and K-value mismatches for EIGRP, and TCP, source-interface and authentication problems for BGP. You will also learn how redistribution can accidentally create routing loops or suboptimal paths if metrics, administrative distance, or route tags are not handled carefully. Throughout the chapter you will use targeted show and debug commands to collect evidence, then apply minimal, safe configuration changes to restore adjacency and correct path selection. Concrete examples include an OSPF adjacency stuck in INIT due to a hello timer mismatch and a mutual redistribution setup that requires a seed metric and the OSPF subnets keyword. By the end, you will be able to interpret adjacency state machines, spot mismatched parameters quickly, and protect redistribution with tags and proper metrics. Consider how a single mismatched timer or forgotten subnets keyword could cause a large outage — this is why disciplined verification and tagging matter.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to diagnose adjacency and peering failures across OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP using targeted verification commands and minimal, safe fixes. You will learn to interpret OSPF neighbor states and identify causes like mismatched hello timers, network types or MTUs. You will also spot EIGRP issues such as AS and K-value mismatches and passive interfaces that stop Hellos. For BGP, you will gain the habit of testing TCP reachability to port 179, verifying remote-as numbers, and confirming update-source and reachability when using loopbacks. Finally, you will design safe redistribution by choosing appropriate seed metrics, applying the OSPF subnets keyword, and using route tags to prevent loops. Each objective pairs a specific show or debug command with a concrete action you can take in a lab or production maintenance window, so you leave with both diagnostic fluency and safe configuration patterns.

This chapter emphasizes concrete application. You will run show and debug commands to collect precise evidence, then make minimal configuration changes to restore normal operation. For OSPF you will practice reading adjacency state transitions and verifying interface parameters such as hello and dead timers, network type and MTU. For EIGRP you will confirm AS numbers, K-values and whether an interface is passive. For BGP you will test TCP reachability to port 179, validate remote-as and update-source when peers use loopbacks, and inspect neighbor details for authentication misconfiguration. In the lab, you will troubleshoot an OSPF adjacency stuck in INIT, correct the timer mismatch, and then configure mutual redistribution between OSPF and EIGRP using a seed metric and the OSPF subnets keyword. Each task includes verification steps such as show ip route, show ip bgp summary, and show ip eigrp neighbors so you can prove routes are learned as expected. These activities mirror real maintenance work where evidence-driven fixes and verification reduce risk.

OSPF neighbors walk through a defined sequence of states before they exchange link-state information. The states are Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading and Full. Each state signals a specific step in neighbor discovery or database synchronization. For example, Init indicates that a Hello packet was received but bidirectional communication hasn’t been established; 2-Way means bidirectional Hello reception has been confirmed, commonly on a multi-access network where DR/BDR elections matter. ExStart and Exchange are where master-slave roles and database description packets are negotiated. If a neighbor stalls in ExStart, a likely culprit is MTU mismatch: routers attempt to exchange DBD packets that the peer cannot process due to packet size differences. Full is the goal — it means complete adjacency and LSDB synchronization. A concrete example: you see a neighbor stuck in INIT on R1. That tells you R2’s Hellos reach R1, but R1’s Hellos are not acknowledged. Start with show ip ospf neighbor and show ip ospf interface to compare timers and interface parameters. A common misconception is to immediately reset interfaces; instead, collect evidence first. The key takeaway is that state transitions narrow the fault domain: read the state, correlate with expected packet exchange, and then target the parameter most likely to differ.

When an OSPF adjacency fails to form, there are a few repeat offenders: mismatched hello or dead timers, inconsistent network types, area ID differences, and authentication mismatches. Each has a distinct troubleshooting pattern. Start with show ip ospf neighbor to see the state. Then use show ip ospf interface to display hello and dead timers, network type, and whether authentication is active. If timers differ, either set the neighbor to the expected default or align both sides to match. Network types such as Broadcast, NBMA or Point-to-Point must agree on each end; a mismatch can prevent adjacency or change DR/BDR expectations. Area IDs must also match for interfaces participating in the same segment; an incorrect area ID isolates the neighbor relationship. Authentication is often overlooked: if one router is configured with authentication and the other is not, or if key chains differ, Hellos will be rejected. A practical approach is a short checklist: check neighbor state, compare timers, verify network type, confirm area ID and inspect authentication settings. A common misconception is assuming only MTU causes ExStart problems; in multi-access segments an incorrect network type can cause 2-Way behavior that prevents full adjacency. Always verify every listed parameter systematically.

MTU mismatch is a subtle but frequent reason OSPF neighbors stall in ExStart. During ExStart/Exchange routers send database description packets which must fit within the peer's MTU. If the peer's MTU is smaller and cannot receive or process the DBD packets, the routers will never progress to Loading and Full. Use show ip interface to inspect interface MTU values and compare both ends. Adjust MTU only when you understand the downstream effects; often fixing tunnel or encapsulation settings that reduce MTU is safer than increasing interface MTU. Another frequent operator error is an access control list that blocks OSPF multicast addresses (224.0.0.5 for AllSPFRouters, 224.0.0.6 for AllDRouters) or blocks unicast packets needed for adjacency negotiation. Before changing ACLs, test connectivity with ping and confirm packet drops with counters. A common misconception is that only multicast must be allowed — OSPF also uses unicast for certain exchanges, and filtering can break adjacency. Always verify with show ip ospf neighbor and debug ip ospf adjacency while in a controlled window. The takeaway is to check MTU and ACLs as part of ExStart troubleshooting and to avoid blind interface resets without evidence.

EIGRP forms neighbors using Hello packets and requires matching Autonomous System numbers. If two routers are intended to be neighbors but do not appear in the neighbor table, the first checks are AS number, interface reachability and whether the interface is configured as passive. The command show ip eigrp neighbors reveals active neighbors; show ip protocols confirms the configured AS. If the AS numbers do not match, routers ignore each other even when IP reachability exists. Another important cause is a passive-interface configuration, which suppresses sending Hellos from that interface and therefore prevents neighbor formation. Authentication mismatches or ACLs blocking EIGRP multicast address 224.0.0.10 also break neighbor discovery. A concrete example: two routers with reachability but no neighbor entry. Run show ip protocols to verify AS, then show ip eigrp interfaces detail to check K-values and interface state. A common misconception is that K-values only affect metric calculation — in fact, mismatched K-values will prevent route exchange even if neighbor adjacency forms. The practical process is: verify AS, check passive-interface and ACLs, then confirm K-values and authentication before assuming a deeper software bug.

EIGRP uses multiple coefficients, known as K-values, to calculate composite metrics. While neighbor formation primarily requires AS match and Hellos, exchanging routes requires compatible metric calculation parameters. If K-values configured on two routers differ, they will not accept route updates from each other. This is sometimes mistaken for a neighbor problem when actually the neighbors are present but routes are refused. To check K-values use show ip eigrp interfaces detail and compare the K-coefficients on participating interfaces. Passive-interface is another common operational setting that disables Hellos on an interface and thus prevents neighbor discovery. Operators sometimes mark an interface passive to stop route advertisements for security; however, if you expect neighbors on that interface, remove passive-interface or limit it to interfaces that should not form neighbors. Authentication mismatches also silently drop updates—always inspect key-chains and match types. A practical troubleshooting sequence: confirm neighbors in show ip eigrp neighbors, check K-values and authentication, and verify passive-interface settings. Closing question: when you see neighbors but no routes, do you check K-values first or authentication? Both are quick checks and together resolve the majority of EIGRP route-exchange issues.

BGP neighbors move through states Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm and Established. These states reflect TCP connection progress and the BGP Open message exchange. When a BGP session never reaches Established, a basic test is to verify TCP reachability to port 179 using telnet or an equivalent test. If TCP cannot connect, an ACL or firewall is likely blocking BGP. If TCP connects but BGP stalls in OpenSent or OpenConfirm, inspect remote-as settings and authentication. The command show ip bgp summary provides a compact view of peer states and prefixes learned, while show ip bgp neighbors gives in-depth information including configured remote-as, authentication and update-source settings. A practical example: a neighbor stuck in Connect indicates TCP cannot complete; telnet <neighbor_ip> 179 fails. Confirm routing reachability with ping, then check ACLs and firewall rules. A common misconception is that BGP problems are always BGP-specific — often they are caused by basic IP reachability or TCP filtering. The diagnostic workflow is: ping the neighbor, test TCP port 179, inspect show ip bgp summary, and finally review neighbor configuration for remote-as and authentication mismatches.

BGP sessions using loopback addresses require explicit source configuration because the TCP session source is not the physical interface IP. The update-source command sets the interface whose IP will be used as the TCP source address. If the neighbor expects a session from the loopback IP but you do not configure update-source, the remote router may reject the connection or fail the remote-as check. Additionally, eBGP peers that are not directly connected need ebgp-multihop to increase the TTL so TCP packets survive intermediate hops. When troubleshooting, verify that the neighbor is IP reachable from the configured source address; use ping with a source when possible and confirm routing to the source. If TCP connects but BGP fails authentication, inspect MD5 key-chains. A practical checklist: confirm reachability to the neighbor IP, verify the update-source is set when using loopbacks, use ebgp-multihop for non-direct eBGP peers, and confirm remote-as numbers match. A common mistake is to forget to route to the loopback source address from the peer, which makes TCP attempts originate from an unreachable IP. Always ensure symmetric reachability and matching TTL settings for eBGP multihop sessions before assuming a BGP implementation bug.

Route-maps and prefix-lists are powerful tools to shape BGP advertisements, but incorrect filters can block all routes unintentionally. The command show ip bgp summary shows prefixes learned; show ip bgp displays the BGP table. When you redistribute, remember that different protocols use different metrics and administrative distances. External routes introduced into another protocol often receive default metrics or higher administrative distance, which affects route selection. We'll walk through the supplied lab scenario: R1 and R2 are connected on GigabitEthernet0/1. R1 runs OSPF Area 0 and R2 runs EIGRP AS 100, but the OSPF adjacency is stuck in INIT. The first diagnostic step is to run show ip ospf neighbor and show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/1 on both routers. These commands will reveal whether Hellos are mismatched. In the given initial configuration, R2 had ip ospf hello-interval 5 while R1 used the default of 10, so R1 saw R2’s Hellos but R2 did not accept R1's, resulting in INIT. Fix the mismatch by setting R2's hello interval to 10 or removing the custom hello command. Verify the adjacency reaches FULL with show ip ospf neighbor. Next, configure EIGRP AS 100 on R2 and advertise its networks. Then perform mutual redistribution on R2: redistribute ospf 1 metric 10000 100 255 1 1500 into EIGRP and redistribute eigrp 100 subnets metric 100 into OSPF. The redistribute commands must include a seed metric for EIGRP and the subnets keyword for OSPF. After configuration, verify route exchange using show ip route on both routers. A common pitfall is forgetting the subnets keyword or not providing a seed metric — both prevent expected route advertisement. Finish by checking that tags are applied if you plan mutual redistribution in production.

Here are the core concepts to internalize. First, OSPF adjacency states are diagnostic: each state tells you what packet exchange has succeeded or failed, so use the state to target your checks. Second, EIGRP K-values control metric compatibility; mismatched K-values can prevent route exchange even when neighbors exist. Third, BGP peering depends on TCP connectivity to port 179 and correct remote-as values; always validate TCP before diving into BGP configuration. Keep these short, testable truths in mind as you work through real networks, because they let you prioritize checks and reduce mean time to repair.
